warmup.text: The race is nearly over. The Lady Wilma reaches Callao, in Peru, and trouble is waiting. Before you read, think of a time a problem turned out to help you. Then set your lens: watch how each fix leads to the next problem.

words.text: This week's roots are curr and curs, which mean run, and tract, which means pull. The spelling pattern is the shun sound at the end of a word. Look at the base word to choose t-i-o-n or s-i-o-n. In the game, every right answer throws a plank in the furnace.

reading.text: Read Chapter 7, End of the Race. Watch the coal. Who has it, who loses it, and what does that cause? Then watch who reminds the captain about the lumber, and listen to how he says it.

assignment.text: Three questions about Chapter 7. Then plan the middle of your adventure. Answer the three questions in a few words each. That is your plan. Then start writing.

Write the second sentence correctly in your reading journal.

how.why: Joining ideas the right way keeps action moving and shows cause and effect.

do: Read the question.
Write 2 or 3 sentences in your reading journal.
Then go on to Word Study.
how.why: Thinking before you read gives you something to watch for.

do: Read the three lenses.
Tap the one you will use today.
Keep it in mind as you read. You will use it at the end.
how.why: Adventure stories run on problems. Each solution causes the next problem.
how.use: You will use it in reading question 1.

do: Read what curr/curs and tract mean.
Read the example words.
Type the missing root in each word, then tap Check Roots.
how.why: Two roots unlock many words about running and pulling.

do: Say each word out loud.
Tap each card to read its meaning.

Think through the questions, then tap Now check your thinking.

how.why: Compound sentences show two things at once; complex ones show cause and effect.

Read the word families.

do: Read the reading focus below.
Open your book and read Chapter 7.
Then do the Read Like a Writer box and the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.
how.why: The pause boxes are places to stop and think while you read.

Answer the three questions in a few words each. That is your plan.
Start writing the middle of your adventure.
how.why: The middle is where the stakes rise. Each fix should lead to a new problem.

glossary.meaning: the push that keeps something moving forward
what happens because of something else

curs: This word is about running before.
The run root that ends in s.
curr: This word is about something that happens, as if it ran into you.
The run root with two r's.

miss.decision: decide ends in de, so it takes -sion: decision.
miss.division: divide ends in de, so it takes -sion: division.
miss.collision: collide ends in de, so it takes -sion: collision.
miss.attraction: attract ends in ct, so it takes -tion.
miss.direction: direct ends in ct, so it takes -tion.
miss.celebration: celebrate ends in te, so it takes -tion.

game.title: Race to the Golden Gate
game.sub: This week's word game · 8 planks today
game.look: It is the last night of the race. The Lady Wilma has no coal, so every right answer throws a plank of lumber into her furnace and she surges toward the Golden Gate. A wrong answer lets the Sea Raven creep up.

do: Read the clue.
Tap the word that really fits.
Watch the Lady Wilma surge ahead.
Tap Full steam.
how.why: The base word tells you -tion or -sion, and a real root tells you the meaning.

game.doneLine: Come back tomorrow for eight more planks.

rounds.clue: The boilers roar. Which spelling names the act of exploding?
rounds.why: explode ends in de, so it takes -sion: explosion.

rounds.clue: Money that runs from hand to hand in San Francisco's shops. Which word has curr (run)?
rounds.why: curr (run) + ency: money that runs from person to person. A curtain only looks like it has the root.

rounds.clue: Writing where the letters run together, like Jack's letter home.
rounds.why: curs (run) + ive: letters that run together.

rounds.clue: Captain Swain checks every inch of his ship. Which spelling names the act of inspecting?
rounds.why: inspect ends in ct, so it takes -tion.
rounds.miss: Look at the end of the base word: inspect.

rounds.clue: Taking one number away from another, as Praiseworthy counts their money.
rounds.why: sub (away) + tract (pull) + ion: pulling one number away from another.

rounds.clue: Which word is in the same family as protect?
rounds.why: protect, protection and protective all share the base protect.

rounds.clue: A builder who signs a deal to put up a hotel in San Francisco.
rounds.why: con (together) + tract (pull) + or: someone who draws a deal together.

rounds.clue: A sudden run into someone else's land.
rounds.why: in (into) + curs (run) + ion: a running in.

virtue.name: generosity
virtue.title: Generosity or not?
virtue.intro: This week's virtue is generosity: giving your time, help or things freely, without asking for anything back. Sort these everyday examples.

items.t: You share your snack with someone who forgot their lunch.
items.why: You give what you have to someone who needs it.

items.t: You help your neighbor carry groceries, then ask for a dollar.
items.why: Helping is kind, but asking to be paid makes it a deal, not a gift.

items.t: You let your little sister have the bigger piece of cake.
items.why: You give up something you wanted so someone else can have it.

items.t: You give away a toy only because it is broken.
items.why: Giving away what you do not want costs you nothing. Generosity gives something that matters.

art.title: Royal Mail Steam Ship Europa
art.alt: A black-and-white print of a long steamship with three masts, sails furled, a tall smokestack and a big paddlewheel on its side, moving through choppy waves.
art.look: A lithograph printed in 1849, the year of the novel. The Europa was a real sidewheel steamship that crossed the Atlantic, not the Pacific. Look at the big paddlewheel on her side, the smokestack and the masts for sails. The made-up Lady Wilma and Sea Raven are the same kind of ship: when the coal runs out, there is nothing to turn the wheel.
